title: Staying in Work Best for Brain Health — Study
paragraphs: Wouldn't it be great to take a break from work — or even retire early? The idea might sound enticing, but research suggests that there may be some drawbacks for your cognitive health.
A study published in Alzheimer's & Dementia looked at 2,400 people taking part in a long-running survey of older Americans called the Health and Retirement Study.

The group involved in this study also answered extra questions about their jobs at least four times between 1998 and 2014. These questions asked about things like whether they were employed or retired, and how worried they were about losing their job in the next year.
In 2016, this group also did cognitive tests that checked for impairment in things like memory and language ability.
And depending on their employment history, some cognitive differences were found.

Among women, those who chose not to work for reasons other than unemployment or retirement showed the greatest signs of cognitive impairment. Early retirement was linked to the second-greatest impairment — though being self-employed was almost as bad, and was actually linked to the worst outcome for language ability.

For men, the greatest cognitive impairment was experienced by those with inconsistent employment — those who made frequent shifts between working, being unemployed and being retired. But retirement — either early or regular — was linked to the second-greatest impairment.
Being self-employed had relatively little connection to cognitive impairment in men, however.

Overall, those who stayed in work showed the least cognitive impairment. This was true even among those who felt the most worried about losing their jobs. In fact, women who were the most worried about losing their jobs actually performed the best in several areas of the cognitive test.

The results point to the cognitive benefits of staying in steady employment. Having a steady job means you spend a lot of your day socializing and problem-solving, both of which may have protective effects on brain health.
And while worrying about losing your job might be stressful, staying in that insecure job might be better for your brain!
